Definition 4.3. The index  $d_0$  of an elliptic fibration  $\pi \colon X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$  is the minimal fibre degree  $d_0 = (C.[X_t])$  of a curve  $C \subset X$  such that  $\pi \colon C \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$  is finite.

Equivalently, the index  $d_0$  is the smallest positive  $\deg(L|_{X_t}) = (L.X_t)$ ,  $L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)$ . Indeed, if  $(L.X_t) &gt; 0$ , then  $H^0(X,L(nX_t)) \neq 0$  for  $n \gg 0$ .

Thus, $\pi \colon X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ admits a section if and only if $d_0 = 1$. Also a complex elliptic K3 surface is projective if and only if $d_0 &lt; \infty$. Indeed, if $D$ is a divisor of positive fibre degree, then $(D + nX_t)^2 &gt; 0$ for $n \gg 0$, cf. page 16 or Remark 8.1.3. See Section 4.3 for more on the non-projective case.

Remark 4.4. Let  $C \subset X$  be of degree  $d_0$  over  $\mathbb{P}^1$ . Then the rational map that sends  $L \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X_t)$  to  $L \otimes \mathcal{O}(C)|_{X_t} \in \operatorname{Pic}^{d + d_0}(X_t)$  extends to an isomorphism of elliptic surfaces

$$
\mathrm {J} ^ {d} (X) \xrightarrow {\sim} \mathrm {J} ^ {d + d _ {0}} (X).
$$

In particular, if  $\pi \colon X\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$  admits a section, then

$$
X \xrightarrow {\sim} \mathrm {J} ^ {d} (X)
$$

for all  $d$

In this sense, the above construction yields at most  $d_0$  different elliptic surfaces

$$
\mathrm {J} ^ {0} (X) = \mathrm {J} (X), \mathrm {J} ^ {1} (X) \simeq X, \dots , \mathrm {J} ^ {d _ {0} - 1} (X).
$$

applying  $\operatorname{Hom}_{X_t}(,L)$  to the exact triangle  $L[1] \longrightarrow i^* i_* L \longrightarrow L$  and using adjunction yields the exact sequence

$$
\operatorname {E x t} _ {X _ {t}} ^ {1} (L, L) \longrightarrow \operatorname {E x t} _ {X} ^ {1} (i _ {*} L, i _ {*} L) \longrightarrow \operatorname {E x t} _ {X _ {t}} ^ {0} (L, L) \longrightarrow \operatorname {E x t} _ {X _ {t}} ^ {2} (L, L).
$$

The morphism in the middle can be interpreted as differential of  $\hat{\pi}$  at  $[L]$ . However, for the locally free  $L$  on the curve  $X_{t}$ , one has  $\operatorname{Ext}_{X_t}^2 (L,L)\simeq H^2 (X_t,\mathcal{O}_{X_t}) = 0$ , i.e.  $\hat{\pi}$  is smooth at  $[L]$ .

Although, these surfaces are usually different, one can nevertheless show that

(4.1) $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)_{t}\simeq X_{t}$

for all $d$ and all closed $t\in\mathbb{P}^{1}$. This is clear for smooth fibres, because then $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)_{t}\simeq\mathrm{Pic}^{d}(X_{t})\simeq X_{t}$ (over the algebraically closed field $k$), and for elliptic surfaces with a section, because then in fact $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\simeq X$ for all $d$. For singular fibres, one reduces to the case with a section by constructing a local (analytic, étale, etc.) section through a smooth point of the fibre $X_{t}$. Here one uses that an elliptic fibration of a K3 surface does not admit multiple fibres. So in fact there exists an open (analytic or étale) covering of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ over which $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ become isomorphic.

Also 

$\mathrm{J}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X))\simeq\mathrm{J}(X)$

for all $d$. Indeed, both elliptic surfaces come with a section and all their fibres are isomorphic. More algebraically, if $E=X_{\eta}$, then all $E_{d}\coloneqq\mathrm{Jac}^{d}(E)$ are torsors under the elliptic curve $E_{0}\coloneqq\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(E)$ by $E_{0}\times E_{d}\mathop{\longrightarrow}E_{d}$, $(M,L)\mathop{\longmapsto}M\otimes L$. However, the curve $E_{d}$ is a torsor under only one elliptic curve, namely its dual, and hence $E_{0}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(E_{d})$, see *[407, Thm. 7.19]* or *[566, X.Thm. 3.8]* and also Section 5.1.

Finally we remark that there are natural rational maps from $X$ to all $\mathrm{J}(X),\ldots,\mathrm{J}^{d_{0}-1}(X)$:

$X\mathop{--}\succ\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$

obtained by mapping a line bundle $L$ of degree one on a smooth fibre $X_{t}$ to $L^{d}$. Use $\mathrm{J}(X)\simeq\mathrm{J}^{d_{0}}(X)$ to get $X\mathop{--}\succ\mathrm{J}(X)$ .

### 4.2

Let us now explain how to use moduli spaces of stable sheaves to give a modular construction for the compactification $\mathrm{J}(X)$ and not only for the open part $\mathrm{Jac}(X/\mathbb{P}^{1})$. This directly proves that $\mathrm{J}(X)$ and in fact all $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$ are K3 surfaces. Moreover, it allows one to control their Picard groups and their periods.

Recall from Chapter 10 the notation $M_{H}(v)$ for the moduli space of semistable sheaves $F$ on $X$ with Mukai vector $v(F)=v$, where semistability is measured with respect to the polarization $H$. If one thinks of a line bundle $L\in\mathrm{Pic}^{d}(X_{t})$ on a fibre $X_{t}$ as a sheaf on $X$, i.e. as $F\coloneqq i_{*}L$, one is led to choose

$v=v_{d}\coloneqq v(i_{*}L)=(0,[X_{t}],d).$

Here, $[X_{t}]$ is the class of the fibre $X_{t}$. It is not hard to see that any line bundle $L$ on a smooth fibre $X_{t}$ gives rise to a sheaf $i_{*}L$ on $X$ that is stable with respect to any $H$. This yields an open immersion

(4.2) $\mathrm{Jac}^{d}((X/\mathbb{P}^{1})_{\mathrm{reg}})\mathop{\longleftarrow}M_{H}(v_{d}),$

where $(X/\mathbb{P}^{1})_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the union of all smooth fibres.

For all choices of $d$ the Mukai vector $v_{d}=(0,[X_{t}],d)$ is primitive and hence for generic $H$ the moduli space $M_{H}(v_{d})$ is a K3 surface, cf. Proposition 10.2.5 and Corollary 10.3.5. But then $M_{H}(v)$ can be taken as the unique minimal model of $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$

Summarizing one obtains the following which can also be deduced from *[131, Thm. 5.3.1]*, cf. Proposition 5.4.

###### Proposition 4.5.

For all $d$, the Jacobian fibration of degree $d$ associated with an elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ defines an elliptic K3 surface $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$. ∎

###### Remark 4.6.

i) The embedding (4.2) can in general not be extended to a modular embedding of $\mathrm{Jac}(X/\mathbb{P}^{1})$ into $M_{H}(v)$. Indeed, a line bundle $L$ on a reducible fibre $X_{t}$ does not necessarily define a stable sheaf $i_{*}L$ on $X$.

ii) The choice of a generic polarization is essential. For example, if $X_{t}$ of type $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ and $H$ restricts to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ on each component, then the fibre of $M_{H}(v_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ over $t$ is of type $\mathrm{I}_{1}$, see *[94, Thm. 6.3.11]*. Choosing a generic polarization blows up the node which results in a $\mathrm{I}_{2}$-fibre as needed to ensure $\mathrm{J}(X)_{t}\simeq X_{t}$.

Combining $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\simeq M_{H}(v_{d})$ with Remark 10.3.7 yields

###### Corollary 4.7.

Let $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be a complex projective elliptic K3 surface and let $v_{d}\coloneqq(0,[X_{t}],d)$, $d\neq 0$. Then there exists an isometry of Hodge structures

(4.3) $H^{2}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X),\mathbb{Z})\simeq v_{d}^{\perp}/\mathbb{Z}\cdot v_{d}.$

In particular, $\rho(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X))=\rho(X)$ for all $d$. ∎

Although $d=0$ is explicitly excluded, the result nevertheless describes also the Hodge structure and Picard group in this case. Indeed, $\mathrm{J}(X)\simeq\mathrm{J}^{d_{0}}(X)$ for $d_{0}$ the index of the elliptic fibration and hence:

(4.4) $H^{2}(\mathrm{J}(X),\mathbb{Z})\simeq v_{d_{0}}^{\perp}/\mathbb{Z}\cdot v_{d_{0}}.$

In *[289]* Keum used the Hodge isometry described by (4.4) to define a lattice embedding $\mathrm{NS}(X)\mathop{\hookrightarrow}\mathrm{NS}(\mathrm{J}(X))$, $\alpha\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{((\alpha.[X_{t}])}/d_{0},\alpha,0)\in v_{d_{0}}^{\perp}/\mathbb{Z}\cdot v_{d_{0}}$ the cokernel of which is generated by $(0,0,1)$. Since $d_{0}\cdot(0,0,1)\in\mathrm{NS}(X)$ under this identification and $d_{0}$ is minimal with this property, one finds (cf. Section 14.0.1)

(4.5) $\mathrm{disc}\,\mathrm{NS}(X)=d_{0}^{2}\cdot\mathrm{disc}\,\mathrm{NS}(\mathrm{J}(X)).$

This immediately yields the following result due to Keum *[289]*.

###### Corollary 4.8.

If $\mathrm{disc}\,\mathrm{NS}(X)$ of an elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is square free, then $\pi$ admits a section. ∎

It is not difficult to generalize (4.5) to arbitrary $d\neq 0$ by describing a common over-lattice for $\mathrm{NS}(X)$ and $\mathrm{NS}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X))$. Eventually, one finds

(4.6) $\mathrm{disc}\,\mathrm{NS}(X)=\mathrm{g.c.d.}(d,d_{0})^{2}\cdot\mathrm{disc}\,\mathrm{NS}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)),$

which sometimes excludes two Jacobians of different degrees $\mathrm{J}^{d_{1}}(X)$ and $\mathrm{J}^{d_{2}}(X)$ from being isomorphic K3 surfaces. See also Example 16.2.11.

Remark 4.9.

As explained above, $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ can be described as moduli spaces. However, the moduli space is not always fine, i.e. there does not always exist a universal sheaf $\mathcal{P}$ on $X\times\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$. In fact, general existence results (see *[264, Cor. 4.6.7]* or Section 10.2.2) assert that a universal family exists whenever the index $d_{0}$ and $d$ are coprime. In this case there exists an equivalence of derived categories

(4.7) $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)),$

see Example 16.2.4.

A universal sheaf always exists étale locally and the obstruction to glue these locally defined universal sheaves yields a class $\alpha_{d}$ in the Brauer group of $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$, see Section 10.2.2. We shall get back to this shortly, see Remark 5.9. In any case, see Section 16.4.1, this then yields an equivalence

(4.8) $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X),\alpha_{d}).$

The equivalence can also be interpreted as saying that $X$ is a fine moduli space of $\alpha_{d}$-twisted sheaves on $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$.

All these observations hold true over any algebraically closed field $k$, which leads to the next remark.

###### Remark 4.10.

The assertions on the Néron–Severi group still hold for elliptic K3 surfaces over arbitrary algebraically closed fields. For $d$ and $d_{0}$ coprime, this can be deduced directly from the equivalence $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X))$ and the induced isometry between their extended Néron–Severi groups

$N(X)\simeq N(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)),$

see Example 16.2.11. This in particular shows that (4.6) continues to hold for elliptic K3 surfaces over arbitrary algebraically closed field at least for $\mathrm{g.c.d.}(d,d_{0})=1$.

### 4.3.

The above algebraic approach is problematic when it comes to non-projective complex elliptic K3 surfaces $\pi\colon X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Nevertheless, it is possible to define the relative Jacobian $\mathrm{J}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and all its relatives $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ also in the complex setting.

Plainly, we cannot work with the Jacobian of the generic fibre and so cannot define $\mathrm{J}(X)$ as the relatively minimal model of it. One can however restrict to the open part of all smooth fibres $\pi\colon(X/\mathbb{P}^{1})_{\mathrm{reg}}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and define $\mathrm{J}((X/\mathbb{P}^{1})_{\mathrm{reg}})$ as the total space of $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}/R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}$. Then one still needs to argue that a (relatively minimal) compactification yielding $\mathrm{J}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ exists, which is not granted on general grounds. Kodaira’s approach is to say that locally analytically $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ has sections, as elliptic K3 surfaces come without multiple fibres, and every (local) elliptic fibration with a section is its own Jacobian fibration. The remaining bit is to glue the local families according to the cocycle for $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}$. We refer to *[32, 184]* and the original paper by Kodaira *[305]*.

A priori, it should be possible to define the $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ as a moduli spaces of sheaves on the fibres of $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ as explained in Section 4.2. However, the theory of moduli spaces of sheaves (especially of torsion sheaves as in our case) on non-projective manifolds has not yet been sufficiently developed to be used here.

## 5. Tate–Šafarevič group

The Tate–Šafarevič group of an elliptic K3 surface $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a section parametrizes all elliptic (K3) surfaces $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ for which $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is isomorphic to the Jacobian fibration $\mathrm{J}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$. The notion is modeled on the Tate–Šafarevič and the Weil–Châtelet group of an elliptic curve, which shall be briefly recalled. The difference between the two groups, however, disappears for K3 surfaces. The algebraic and the complex approach to the Tate–Šafarevič group are quite similar, but in the latter context also non-algebraic surfaces are parametrized. Both versions are presented, using the occasion to practice the different languages.

### 5.1.

Let us start with the Weil–Châtelet group of an elliptic curve $E_{0}$ over a field $K$, where $K$ later is the function field $k(t)$ of $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}$ with $k$ algebraically closed (or a finite field).

A *torsor* under $E_{0}$ is a smooth projective curve of genus one over $K$ together with a simply transitive action

$E_{0}\times E\!\longrightarrow\!E,\ (p,x)\!\longrightarrow\!p+x.$

Isomorphisms of $E_{0}$-torsors are defined in the obvious manner. In particular, $E$ is isomorphic to the trivial torsor $E_{0}$ if and only if $E(K)\neq\emptyset$. Then the *Weil–Châtelet group* is the set

$\mathrm{WC}(E_{0})\coloneqq\{E=E_{0}\text{-torsor}\}/_{\simeq}.$

This groups contains the Tate–Šafarevič group $\mathrm{III}(E_{0})$ as a subgroup, which is in general a proper subgroup. As in our applications both groups coincide, we do not go into the definition of $\mathrm{III}(E_{0})$.

If $E$ is an $E_{0}$-torsor, then $E_{0}\simeq\mathrm{Jac}(E)$ as algebraic groups. Indeed, choose any $x\in E(K^{\prime})$ for some finite extension $K^{\prime}/K$ and define $E_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Jac}(E)$, $p\!\longmapsto\!\mathcal{O}_{E}((p+x)-x)$, which is an isomorphism over $K$. For an isomorphism $f\colon E\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}E^{\prime}$ of $E_{0}$-torsors this isomorphism changes by $f_{*}$. Conversely, if a group isomorphism $E_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Jac}(E)$, $p\!\longmapsto\!L_{p}$, is given, then define $E_{0}\times E\!\longrightarrow\!E$, $(p,x)\!\longmapsto\!y$ with $y$ the unique point satisfying $\mathcal{O}(x)\otimes L_{p}\simeq\mathcal{O}(y)$. This turns $E$ into an $E_{0}$-torsor. As a result, one obtains a natural bijection

(5.1) $\mathrm{WC}(E_{0})\simeq\{(E,\varphi)\ |\ \varphi\colon E_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Jac}(E)\}/_{\simeq},$

where $(E,\varphi)\simeq(E^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime})$ if there exists an isomorphism $f\colon E\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}E^{\prime}$ with $f_{*}\circ\varphi=\varphi^{\prime}$. A cohomological description of the Weil–Châtelet group is provided by the next result.

###### Proposition 5.1.

There exists a natural bijection

(5.2) $\mathrm{WC}(E_{0})\simeq H^{1}(K,E_{0}).$

Here, $H^{1}(K,E_{0})\coloneqq H^{1}(\operatorname{Gal}(\bar{K}/K),E_{0}(\bar{K}))$ is the Galois cohomology of $E_{0}$, where $\bar{K}$ denotes the separable closure of $K$.

###### Proof.

For any $E_{0}$-torsor $E$ the Galois group $G\coloneqq\operatorname{Gal}(\bar{K}/K)$ acts naturally on $E(\bar{K})$. If $x\in E(\bar{K})$, then $G\mathop{\longrightarrow}E_{0}(\bar{K})$, $g\mathop{\longmapsto}p_{g}$ with $g\cdot x=p_{g}+x$ defines a continuous crossed homomorphism and thus an element in $H^{1}(G,E_{0}(\bar{K}))$. Choosing a different point $x^{\prime}\in E(\bar{K})$ the crossed homomorphism differs by a boundary. Hence, there is a well-defined map $\operatorname{WC}(E_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{1}(G,E_{0}(\bar{K}))$.

Conversely, a crossed homomorphism $G\mathop{\longrightarrow}E_{0}(\bar{K})$, $g\mathop{\longmapsto}p_{g}$, yields for all $g$ an isomorphism $\varphi_{g}\colon E_{0}\times\bar{K}\mathop{\longrightarrow}E_{0}\times\bar{K}$, $\varphi_{g}(x)=p_{g}+x$. The isomorphisms $\varphi_{g}$ satisfy the cocycle condition $\varphi_{g}\cdot(g\cdot\varphi_{h})=\varphi_{gh}$ and thus define a descent datum, which in turn yields $E$ over $K$ that splits the descent datum after extension to $\bar{K}$. one does not really need the full machinery of descent at this point, as smooth curves are uniquely determined by their function field and it suffices to construct $K(E)$ by descent. See *[407, Ch. IV.7]* or *[566, Ch. X]* for details and references. ∎

The right hand side of (5.2) has the structure of an abelian group. The induced group structure on the left hand side has the property that the product $E_{3}$ of two $E_{0}$-torsors $E_{1}$, $E_{2}$ comes with a morphism $\psi\colon E_{1}\times E_{2}\mathop{\longrightarrow}E_{3}$ satisfying $\psi(p+x_{1},q+x_{2})\mathop{\longrightarrow}(p+q)+\psi(x_{1},x_{2})$, see *[566, p. 355]*.

###### Remark 5.2.

Let $E$ be an $E_{0}$-torsor and so $\operatorname{Jac}(E)\simeq E_{0}$. Then, $\operatorname{Jac}^{d}(E)$ (see Section 4.1) admits canonically the structure of an $E_{0}$-torsor, i.e.

$\operatorname{Jac}^{d}(E)\in\operatorname{WC}(\operatorname{Jac}(E)).$

Using the group structure of $\operatorname{WC}(E_{0})$ and writing $E\simeq\operatorname{Jac}^{1}(E)$, one finds that $[\operatorname{Jac}^{d}(E)]=d\cdot[E]\in\operatorname{WC}(E_{0})$. Indeed, $\operatorname{Jac}^{d_{1}}(E)\times\operatorname{Jac}^{d_{2}}(E)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\operatorname{Jac}^{d_{1}+d_{2}}(E)$, $(L,M)\mathop{\longmapsto}L\otimes M$ satisfies the above property with respect to the natural action of $\operatorname{Jac}(E)$.

The Weil–Châtelet group can be defined more generally for any group scheme, e.g. for the smooth part $X^{\prime}_{t}$ of a singular fibre $X_{t}$ of an elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$, see Section 2.5. So, in particular, one can speak of $\operatorname{WC}(X^{\prime}_{t})$. However, over an algebraically closed field $k$ this group is trivial and only when put in families it becomes interesting. It leads to the notion of the Weil–Châtelet group of an elliptic surface, see below.

### 5.2.

Let $\pi\colon X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an elliptic K3 surface with a section $C_{0}\subset X_{0}$. We shall work over an algebraically closed field $k$, but the arguments remain valid for $k=\mathbb{F}_{q}$.

Consider the open set $X^{\prime}_{0}\subset X_{0}$ of $\pi$-smooth points as a group scheme $X^{\prime}_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$, see Section 2.5. A torsor under $X^{\prime}_{0}$ is defined similarly to the absolute case as a smooth fibration $X^{\prime}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a group action

$X^{\prime}_{0}\times_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}X^{\prime}\mathop{\longrightarrow}X^{\prime},$

making the fibres $X^{\prime}_{t}$ torsors under $(X^{\prime}_{0})_{t}$. The set of all $X^{\prime}_{0}$-torsors is the Weil–Châtelet group of $X_{0}$, but due to the absence of multiple fibres, it equals the Tate–Šafarevič group of $X_{0}$ and we shall, therefore, not distinguish between the two.

###### Definition 5.3.

The *Tate–Šafarevič group* of an elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a section is the set of all torsors under the group scheme $X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$:

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\coloneqq\{(X^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1})=(X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1})\text{-torsor}\}/_{\simeq}.$

The next result is the converse of Proposition 4.5. It allows us to interprete $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ in terms of Jacobian fibrations.

###### Proposition 5.4.

Let $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be a relatively minimal elliptic surface such that its Jacobian $X_{0}\coloneqq\mathrm{J}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is a K3 surface. Then $X$ is a K3 surface itself.

###### Proof.

There are various approaches to the assertion. The first one is to view $X$ as a moduli space of twisted sheaves on $X_{0}$, cf. Remarks 4.9 and 5.9. This, in the spirit of the arguments used to prove Proposition 4.5, would essentially immediately show that $X$ is a K3 surface.

The second approach uses the observation that étale locally $\mathrm{J}(X)$ and $X$ are isomorphic if in addition one assumes the existence of local sections also for $X$, i.e. that $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ has no multiple fibres. This then implies $e(\mathrm{J}(X))=e(X)=24$ and hence $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}(-2)$. (In *[131, Prop. 5.3.6]* this is proved without the additional assumption on $X$.) The general canonical bundle formula for elliptic fibrations yields $\omega_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{X}$. Moreover, $\chi(\mathcal{O}_{X})=2$ and hence $h^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})=0$. Altogether this indeed proves that $X$ is a K3 surface.

For yet another approach in the case of complex K3 surfaces see Remark 5.15. ∎

For the following by definition the generic fibre $E$ of a torsor $X^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ under $X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is a torsor under the generic fibre $E_{0}$ of $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and so $\mathrm{Jac}(E)\simeq E_{0}$.

###### Corollary 5.5.

Let $\pi\colon X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an elliptic K3 surface with a section and let $E_{0}$ be its generic fibre.

1. Taking the generic fibre of a torsor under $X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ (the open part of $\pi$-smooth points) defines an isomorphism

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{WC}(E_{0}).$
2. The Tate–Šafarevič group $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ can be naturally identified with the set of pairs $(X,\varphi)$ with $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ an elliptic K3 surface and an isomorphism $\varphi\colon X_{0}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{J}(X)$ over $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ respecting the group scheme structures on $X_{0}^{\prime}$ and $\mathrm{J}(X)^{\prime}$.

###### Proof.

(i) An $E_{0}$-torsor $E$ is trivial if and only if it admits a $K$-rational point. Similarly, a $(X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1})$-torsor $X^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is trivial if and only if it admits a section. Now, if the generic fibre $E$ of $X^{\prime}$ admits a $K$-rational point, then its closure in $X^{\prime}$ defines a section. Hence, $X^{\prime}\!\longmapsto\!E$ defines an injection $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{WC}(E_{0})$.

To prove surjectivity, one considers the relatively minimal model $X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of an $E_{0}$-torsor $E$. Then $\mathrm{J}(X)\simeq X_{0}$ and, hence, $X$ is a K3 surface. However, for an elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ the $\pi$-smooth part $X^{\prime}$ is a torsor under $\mathrm{J}(X)^{\prime}$. This is the global version of the observation (4.1) that $X_{t}\simeq\mathrm{J}(X)_{t}$ for all $t$.

######

(ii) Combine (5.1) with (i) and the proposition. Once more, one uses the uniqueness of the minimal model to extend $E_{0}\simeq\mathrm{Jac}(E)$ to an isomorphism $X_{0}\simeq\mathrm{J}(X)$. ∎

The reason behind the isomorphism between the Weil–Châtelet groups of the surface and the generic fibre is the absence of multiple fibres in an elliptic fibration of a K3 surface. The situation is more involved for arbitrary elliptic surfaces.

###### Proposition 5.6.

Let $\pi\colon X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an elliptic K3 surface with a section $C_{0}\subset X_{0}$. Then there exist natural isomorphisms

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})\simeq\mathrm{Br}(X_{0}).$

###### Proof.

The proof, inspired by the discussion of Friedman and Morgan in *[184]*, is split in three parts. See also *[603, Ch. 5.3]*. We work in the étale topology.

i) There exists a natural isomorphism

(5.3) $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}).$

This holds without the assumption that there exists a section and follows from the Leray spectral sequence $E_{2}^{p,q}=H^{p}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{q}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m})\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})$ and the following facts: $\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}\simeq\mathbb{G}_{m}$ (which is proved similarly to $\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}$), $R^{2}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}=0$ (see *[225, III.Cor. 3.2]*), and $H^{q}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathbb{G}_{m})=0$ for $q\geq 2$ (see *[140, III.Prop. 3.1]*).

ii) Denote by $\mathcal{X}_{0}$ the sheaf of étale local sections $\sigma\colon U\!\longrightarrow\!X_{0}$ of $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ or, equivalently, of $X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Since the latter is a group scheme, $\mathcal{X}_{0}$ is indeed a sheaf of abelian groups on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Then

(5.4) $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0}).$

This is the relative version of Proposition 5.1 and proved analogously.

iii) The sheaf $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is associated with the presheaf $U\!\longmapsto\!\mathrm{Pic}(X_{0}\times_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}U)$. Using this, one defines a natural sheaf homomorphism

$\mathcal{X}_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m},\ \sigma\!\longmapsto\!\mathcal{O}(\sigma(U)-C_{0}|_{U}).$

Here, $\sigma$ is a section of $X_{0}^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ over the étale open set $U$ and $\sigma(U)$ and $C_{0}|_{U}$ are considered as divisors on $X_{0}\times_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}U$. This sheaf homomorphism is injective, because different points on smooth fibres are never linearly equivalent, and in fact induces an isomorphism

(5.5) $H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}).$

To prove this, note first that the subgroups of vertical divisors in $\mathrm{Pic}(X_{0}\times_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}U)$ form a subsheaf of $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ concentrated in the finitely many singular values $t\in\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of $\pi$. Hence, $H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}/_{\mathrm{vert}})$. Now the cokernel of the induced injection $\mathcal{X}_{0}\!\hookrightarrow\!R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}/_{\mathrm{vert}}$ is just $\mathbb{Z}$, measuring the fibre degree. Taking $H^{1}$ yields (5.5), as $H^{1}_{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathbb{Z})=0$ and $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}/_{\mathrm{vert}})\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{Z}$ is surjective, for $\mathcal{O}(C_{0})\!\longmapsto\!1$.

Composing (5.3) with (5.5) and (5.4) proves the first isomorphism of the proposition. For the second see Section 18.1.1. ∎

###### Corollary 5.7.

The Tate–Šafarevič group $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is a torsion group.

###### Proof.

roof. This can, of course, be seen as a consequence of $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})$, as the latter is known to be torsion, see Example LABEL:eq:1.4.

However, one can also argue geometrically as follows: Let $(X,\varphi)\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$, i.e. $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is an elliptic K3 surface with $\varphi\colon X_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits}\mathrm{J}(X)$. Then $d\cdot[(X,\varphi)]$ is represented by $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ (see Remark 5.2) and $\mathrm{J}^{d_{0}}(X)\simeq\mathrm{J}(X)$ if $d_{0}$ is the index of the elliptic fibration $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$, see Remark 4.4. Hence, $[(X,\varphi)]\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is of finite order dividing $d_{0}$. (In fact, it is of order exactly $d_{0}$, see Remark 5.9.) ∎

Despite this result, $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is difficult to grasp. For complex K3 surfaces the analytic description of the Brauer group gives some insight, but over other fields, e.g. finite ones, the Tate–Šafarevič group remains elusive.

###### Remark 5.8.

In the proof of the proposition we used the sheaf of étale local sections $\mathcal{X}_{0}$ of the elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and the isomorphism $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0})$, see (5.4). On the other hand, the Mordell–Weil group $\mathrm{MW}(X_{0})$ is by definition $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0})$, so Mordell–Weil group and Tate–Šafarevič group are cohomology groups of the same sheaf on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Let us elaborate on this a little more.

Fibrewise multiplication by $n$ yields a short exact sequence

$0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{X}_{0}[n]\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{X}_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{X}_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0,$

where $\mathcal{X}_{0}[n]$ is the sheaf of sections through $n$-torsion points in the fibres. Taking the long exact cohomology sequence gives the exact sequence

$0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{MW}(X_{0})/n\cdot\mathrm{MW}(X_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0}[n])\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{III}(X_{0})[n]\mathop{\longrightarrow}0.$

Here, $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})[n]\subset\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is the subgroup of elements of order dividing $n$. The cohomology $H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0}[n])$ linking $\mathrm{MW}(X_{0})$ and $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is the analogue of the Selmer group of an elliptic curve for the elliptic K3 surface $\pi\colon X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$. So one could introduce

$S^{n}(X_{0})\coloneqq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0}[n])$

and call it the Selmer group of the elliptic surface $\pi\colon X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$.

###### Remark 5.9.

For $\alpha\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$, let $\pi\colon X_{\alpha}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be the associated elliptic K3 surface together with the natural isomorphism $\mathrm{J}(X_{\alpha})\simeq X_{0}$. The techniques in the proof of Proposition 5.6 yield an exact sequence, see also *[225, (4.35)]* or *[20, Prop. 1.6]*,

$0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{X}_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}_{m}/_{\mathrm{vert}}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0,$

which splits for trivial $\alpha$. For general $\alpha$, taking cohomology one obtains an exact sequence

$\mathrm{Pic}(X_{\alpha})\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathbb{G}/_{\mathrm{vert}}).$

By definition, the image of $\mathrm{Pic}(X_{\alpha})\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}$ is generated by the index $d_{0}$ and the boundary of $\bar{1}\in\mathbb{Z}/d_{0}\mathbb{Z}$ yields $\alpha\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$. In particular, $d_{0}$ is the order of $\alpha\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq\mathrm{Br}(X_{0})$. Moreover, as in the proof of Proposition 5.6, one obtains the short exact sequence

(5.6) $0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\langle\alpha\rangle\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{Br}(X_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{Br}(X_{\alpha})\mathop{\longrightarrow}0.$

This is a special case of (2.1) in Section 10.2.2.

Viewing $\mathrm{J}(X_{\alpha})\simeq X_{0}$ as the moduli space of sheaves on $X_{\alpha}$, the class $\alpha$ can also be interpreted as the obstruction class to the existence of a universal sheaf on $X_{0}\times X_{\alpha}$ and hence by (4.8)

$\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X_{0},\alpha)\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X_{\alpha}).$

Donagi and Pantev in *[154]* generalized this equivalence to

(5.7) $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X_{\beta},\bar{\alpha})\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X_{\alpha},\bar{\beta}),$

for arbitrary $\alpha,\beta\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$. Here, $\bar{\alpha},\bar{\beta}$ denote their images under the natural maps $\mathrm{Br}(X_{0})\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{Br}(X_{\beta})$ and $\mathrm{Br}(X_{0})\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{Br}(X_{\alpha})$, respectively.

The following special case of (5.7) has been observed earlier. Consider the elliptic K3 surface $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X_{\alpha})$. As has been explained before, there is a natural isomorphism $\mathrm{J}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X_{\alpha}))\simeq\mathrm{J}(X_{\alpha})\simeq X_{0}$. Thus, $\mathrm{J}^{d}(X_{\alpha})$ corresponds to some class $\beta\in\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ and in fact $\beta=d\alpha$. Therefore, in this case $\bar{\beta}$ is trivial and (5.7) becomes $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{J}^{d}(X),\alpha_{d})\simeq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(X)$ with $X=X_{\alpha}$ and $\alpha_{d}=\bar{\alpha}$, as in (4.8).

###### Remark 5.10.

The famous conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer (see the announcement as one of the Clay Milllenium Problems by Wiles in *[633]*) predicts that for an elliptic curve over a number field $K$ the rank of the Mordell–Weil group $E(K)$ equals the order of the $L$-series $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$. Its generalization links the first non-trivial coefficient of the Taylor expansion of $L(E,s)$ to the order of the Tate–Šafarevič group $\mathrm{III}(E)$. In particular, $\mathrm{III}(E)$ is expected to be finite.

The function field analogue of it leads to the conjecture that for an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}(t)$ the Tate–Šafarevič group $\mathrm{III}(E)$ should be finite. Combined with Proposition 5.6 it therefore predicts that for an elliptic K3 surface $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ the Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(X_{0})$ is finite. This has been generalized by Artin and Tate to the conjecture that the Brauer group of any surface over a finite field should be finite, see Tate’s *[593, Sec. 1]* and the discussion in Section 18.2.2, especially Remark 18.2.9.

### 5.3.

We change the setting and consider complex elliptic K3 surfaces $\pi\colon X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Recall that $X$ is projective if and only if its index (cf. Definition 4.3) $d_{0}$ is finite. In particular, an elliptic K3 surface $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a section $C_{0}$ is always algebraic. Analogously to the definition of $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ in the algebraic setting one has:

###### Definition 5.11.

The *analytic Tate–Šafarevič group* $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$ of a complex elliptic K3 surface $X_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a section is the set of elliptic K3 surfaces $\pi\colon X\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ such that the $\pi$-smooth part $X^{\prime}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is endowed with the structure of an $X^{\prime}_{0}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{P}^{1}$ torsor.

We stress that, although $X_{0}$ is algebraic, an elliptic K3 surface $X$ representing an element in $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$ may very well be non-algebraic. However, as in Proposition 5.4, $X$ is automatically a K3 surface. Arguing via moduli spaces of twisted sheaves is tricky in the non-algebraic setting, but the fact that $X$ and $\mathrm{J}(X)$ are locally (this time in the analytic topology) isomorphic fibrations still holds. See also Remark 5.15.

Most of what has been said above in the algebraic setting holds true in the analytic one, by replacing étale topology, cohomology etc., by their analytic versions. However,

there are also striking differences, as becomes clear immediately. Firstly, the proof of Proposition 5.6 goes through in the analytic version and the asserted isomorphism then reads (see also *[514, Ch. VII.8]*)

(5.8) $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*}).$

In fact, the intermediate isomorphisms (5.4), (5.4), and (5.5) also hold:

$\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{X}_{0}^{\mathrm{an}})\simeq H^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*}).$

Here, $\mathcal{X}_{0}^{\mathrm{an}}$ denotes the sheaf of analytic sections of $X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$.

###### Corollary 5.12.

For a complex elliptic K3 surface $X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with a section there exists a short exact sequence

$0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{NS}(X_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{Z})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\mathop{\longrightarrow}0.$

In particular,

$\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\simeq\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}^{22-\rho(X_{0})}.$

###### Proof.

This follows from the exponential sequence, $H^{3}(X_{0},\mathbb{Z})=0$, and (5.8). ∎

###### Remark 5.13.

The standard comparison of the analytic cohomology of $\mathcal{O}^{*}$ with the étale cohomology of $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ relates the analytic with the algebraic Tate–Šafarevič group. As a motivation, start with the well-known

(5.9) $H^{1}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})\simeq H^{1}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*}).$

The two sides are naturally isomorphic to $\mathrm{Pic}(X_{0})$, which is the same for both topologies. However, in degree two this becomes

$H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})_{\mathrm{tors}}$

and hence

(5.10) $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})_{\mathrm{tors}}.$

To prove (5.10), we use the usual comparison morphism $\xi\colon H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})$, the Kummer sequence $0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mu_{n}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{G}_{m}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{G}_{m}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0$, and the fact that étale and analytic cohomology coincide for finite abelian groups. This then yields immediately that $\xi$ surjects onto the torsion of $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})$. To prove injectivity, apply (5.9) and the fact that $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{G}_{m})$ is torsion. (The latter follows from Corollary 5.7 for elliptic $X_{0}$, but of course holds in general for the Brauer group of a smooth surface, see Section 18.1.1.)

In particular, one finds (see Section 18.1.2)

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})^{22-\rho(X_{0})}.$

The identification

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})_{\mathrm{tors}}\subset\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$

can also be explained geometrically. Clearly, one has a natural inclusion $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\subset\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$ and we have remarked already that $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$ is torsion. On the other hand, if $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ defines a torsion class in $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$, then there exists a finite $d>0$ such that

$\mathrm{J}^{d}(X)$ admits a section, see proof of Corollary 5.7. This section gives rise to a line bundle of degree $d$ on each fibre which then can be shown to glue to a line bundle $L$ on $X$. Moreover, $\pi_{*}L\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(n)$ for $n\gg 0$ admits non-trivial global sections. Interpreted as sections of $L\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(n)$, their zero sets are divisors on $X$ of positive fibre degree. Hence $X$ is algebraic and, therefore, is contained in $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$.

###### Remark 5.14.

 for a non-algebraic elliptic K3 surface $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ its generic fibre $E$ is ill defined. However, as $\mathrm{J}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is always algebraic, $\mathrm{Jac}(E)$ makes perfect sense nevertheless.

###### Remark 5.15.

The surjection

$H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})\simeq\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$

allows one to write down (however, not effectively) a family of elliptic surfaces over the line $\mathbb{C}\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})$ parametrizing all elliptic surfaces $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with $\mathrm{J}(X)\simeq X_{0}$.

A sketch of the argument can be found in *[184, Ch. 1.5]*, it roughly goes as follows: Pick a fine enough open cover $\mathbb{P}^{1}=\bigcup U_{i}$ such that classes in

$H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})\simeq H^{1}(X_{0},R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})$

can be represented by sections of $R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}$ over $U_{i}\cap U_{j}$ and such that for every singular fibre $X_{t}$ there exists a unique $U_{i}$ containing $t$. Now use

$R^{1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}|_{U_{i}\cap U_{j}}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{an}}_{0}|_{U_{i}\cap U_{j}}$

to translate the glueing maps over $U_{i}\cap U_{j}$ defining $X_{0}$ by the section of $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{an}}_{0}$ obtained as images of classes in $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})$. This yields new elliptic surfaces and one checks that their classes in $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\simeq H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})$ are given by the image under the exponential map $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}}^{*})$.

It is worth noting that the family constructed in this way really is a family of elliptic surfaces, i.e. it comes with compatible projections to $\mathbb{P}^{1}$. Also this approach to $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$ shows that all elliptic surfaces $X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ in $\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$ (and so in particular all in $\mathrm{III}(X_{0})$) are deformation equivalent to $X_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and, therefore, are K3 surfaces as well. This is an alternative argument for Proposition 5.4 when $k=\mathbb{C}$. In this family, the algebraic surfaces are dense, because

$\mathrm{III}(X_{0})\simeq(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})^{22-\rho(X_{0})}\subset\mathrm{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})\simeq\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}^{22-\rho(X_{0})}$

induced by $H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{Q})\mathop{\hookleftarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathbb{R})\mathop{\longrightarrow}H^{2}(X_{0},\mathcal{O}_{X_{0}})\simeq\mathbb{C}$ is dense.

References and further reading:

In practice, it can be very difficult to determine or describe all elliptic fibrations of a given K3 surface. This is only partially due to the automorphism group. For Kummer surfaces associated with the Jacobian $\mathrm{Jac}(C)$ of a generic genus two curve $C$ this was recently studied in detail by Kumar in *[337]*. For elliptic fibrations of Kummer surfaces associated with a product of

elliptic curves see *[342, 457, 464]* and *[295]* for elliptic fibrations of a generic double plane with ramification over six lines.

Is a semistable (i.e. only I_{n}-fibres occur) extremal elliptic K3 surface determined by its configuration of singular fibres? This question has been treated by Miranda and Persson *[414]* and Artal Bartolo, Tokunaga, and Zhang *[12]*, in the latter article one finds more on the possible Mordell–Weil groups. In *[339]* Kuwata exhibits examples of elliptic quartic surfaces with Mordell–Weil groups of rank at least 12.

The description of NS(J($X$)) by Keum *[289]* was motivated by Belcastro’s thesis *[56]*. However, in the latter J($X$) was linked to a moduli space of bundles with Mukai vector $(d_{0},[X_{t}],0)$. The relation between the two approaches can be explained in terms of elementary transformations as in Section 9.2.2 or, more abstractly, by the spherical twist $T_{\mathcal{O}}$, see Section 16.2.3.

Questions and open problems:

To the best of my knowledge, not all of the statements for complex elliptic K3 surfaces that should hold as well in positive characteristic have actually been worked out in full detail, see e.g. Remarks 3.11 and 4.10.

It would be interesting to compute periods of non-projective $(X\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{P}^{1})\in\mathds{III}^{\mathrm{an}}(X_{0})$.

As mentioned in Section 4.3, there are things left to check to view J${}^{d}(X)$ as moduli space of sheaves in the non-algebraic setting.

Chapter 12 Chow ring and Grothendieck group

This chapter starts with a quick review of the basic facts on Chow and Grothendieck groups. In particular, we mention Roitman’s result about torsion freeness, which we formulate only for K3 surfaces, and prove divisibility of the homologically trivial part. Section 2 outlines Mumford’s result about $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ being big for complex K3 surfaces and contrasts it with the Bloch–Beĭlinson conjecture for K3 surfaces over number fields. This section also contains two approaches, due to Bloch and Green–Griffiths–Paranjape, to prove that $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ grows under transcendental base field extension. The last section discusses more recent results of Beauville and Voisin on a natural subring of $\mathrm{CH}^{*}(X)$ that naturally splits the cycle map.

### 1.1. General facts on $\mathrm{CH}^{*}(X)$ and $K(X)$

We consider an algebraic K3 surface $X$ over an arbitrary field $k$ and study its Chow ring $\mathrm{CH}^{*}(X)$ and its Grothendieck group $K(X)$. In this first section we recall standard definitions and results and explain what they say for K3 surfaces.

#### 1.1.1.

The ultimate reference for intersection theory and Chow groups is Fulton’s book *[190]*. A brief outline summarizing the basic functorial properties of the Chow ring can be found in *[234, App. A]*.

For an arbitrary variety $Y$ over a field $k$, a cycle of codimension $n$ is a finite linear combination $Z=\sum n_{i}[Z_{i}]$ with $n_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $Z_{i}\subset Y$ closed integral subvarieties of codimension $n$. The group of all such cycles shall be denoted $Z^{n}(Y)$.

Let $\nu\colon\tilde{V}\!\longrightarrow\!V\subset Y$ be the normalization of a subvariety $V\subset Y$. Recall that two divisors $D,D^{\prime}$ on $\tilde{V}$, i.e. cycles of codimension one on the normal variety $\tilde{V}$, are linearly equivalent if $D-D^{\prime}$ is a principal divisor (which for Cartier divisor is equivalent to $\mathcal{O}(D)\simeq\mathcal{O}(D^{\prime})$). In this case, the image cycles $Z\coloneqq\nu_{*}D$ and $Z^{\prime}\coloneqq\nu_{*}D^{\prime}$ on $Y$ are called rationally equivalent. The equivalence relation generated by this is rational equivalence and is denoted $Z\sim Z^{\prime}$.

The Chow group of cycles of codimension $n$ on a variety $Y$ is by definition the group of all cycles of codimension $n$ modulo rational equivalence:

$\mathrm{CH}^{n}(Y)\coloneqq Z^{n}(Y)/_{\sim}.$

For a smooth variety $Y$ the map $D\!\longmapsto\!\mathcal{O}(D)$ yields an injection $\mathrm{CH}^{1}(Y)\!\hookrightarrow\!\mathrm{Pic}(Y)$ (by definition rational equivalence equals linear equivalence for codimension one cycles), which is in fact an isomorphism for integral $Y$, see *[234, II.Prop. 6.15]*. One can define the first Chern class $\mathrm{c_{1}}\colon\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{1}(Y)$ as its inverse.

12. CHOW RING AND GROTHENDIECK GROUP

For a smooth quasi-projective variety $Y$ it is possible to define the intersection of cycles modulo rational equivalence which endows

$$
\mathrm{CH}^*(Y) := \bigoplus \mathrm{CH}^n(Y)
$$

with the structure of a graded commutative ring. For two subvarieties $Z, Z' \subset Y$ meeting transversally this is given by the naive intersection $Z \cap Z'$. If the two subvarieties do not intersect transversally or even in the wrong codimension, one needs to deform them first according to Chow's moving lemma (for algebraically closed $k$) which requires working modulo rational equivalence, cf. [190, Ch. 11] or [617, 21.2]. Another approach to the intersection product uses deformation to the normal cone.

If $Y$ is of dimension $d$, then any $Z \in \mathrm{CH}^d(Y)$ can be written as a finite sum $Z = \sum n_i[y_i]$ with closed points $y_i \in Y$. The degree of $Z$ is then defined as

$$
\deg \left(\sum n_i[y_i]\right) := \sum n_i[k(y_i):k],
$$

which does not depend on the chosen representative. It defines a group homomorphism

$$
\deg \colon \mathrm{CH}^d(Y) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z},
$$

the kernel of which is denoted

$$
\mathrm{CH}^d(Y)_0 := \operatorname{Ker} \left(\deg \colon \mathrm{CH}^d(Y) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}\right).
$$

Let us now specialize to the case that $Y$ is a K3 surface $X$. For dimension reasons one has

$$
\mathrm{CH}^*(X) = \mathrm{CH}^0(X) \oplus \mathrm{CH}^1(X) \oplus \mathrm{CH}^2(X).
$$

Clearly, $\mathrm{CH}^0(X) \simeq \mathbb{Z}$, which is naturally generated by $[X]$, and $\mathrm{CH}^1(X) \simeq \operatorname{Pic}(X)$ via the first Chern class.¹

**Remark 1.1.** For $k = \bar{k}$ rational equivalence of 0-cycles can be understood more explicitly as follows. A cycle $Z$ of codimension zero is rationally equivalent to 0 if there exists a morphism $f\colon \mathbb{P}^1 \longrightarrow S^n(X)$ such that $f(0) - f(\infty) = Z$. The equivalence relation generated by this condition really is rational equivalence. Here, $S^n(X)$ denotes the symmetric product of the surface $X$, cf. Section 10.3.3, and the cycle $f(t)$ is $\sum [x_i]$ if the image of $t$ under $f$ is the point $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in S^n(X)$, see [190, Ex. 1.6.3] or [437].

The intersection product with $\mathrm{CH}^0(X) = \mathbb{Z}$ is obvious and for dimension reasons $\mathrm{CH}^2(X)$ intersects trivially with $\mathrm{CH}^1(X) \oplus \mathrm{CH}^2(X)$. Thus, the only interesting intersection product on a surface $X$ is

$$
\mathrm{CH}^1(X) \times \mathrm{CH}^1(X) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^2(X).
$$

If $C_1, C_2 \subset X$ are two curves, then $[C_1] \cdot [C_2] \in \mathrm{CH}^2(X)$ can be described as the image $\nu_*[D]$ under the normalization $\nu \colon \tilde{C}_1 \longrightarrow C_1 \subset X$ of any divisor $D$ with $\mathcal{O}(D) \simeq \nu^*\mathcal{O}(C_2)$.

¹For a complex non-projective K3 surface $X$ it might happen that $X$ does not contain any curve, and in this sense $Z^1(X) = 0$ and $\mathrm{CH}^1(X) = 0$, but nevertheless one could have $\operatorname{Pic}(X) \neq 0$. For example, consider a K3 surface with $\operatorname{Pic}(X) = \mathrm{NS}(X)$ generated by a line bundle $L$ with $(L)^2 = -4$, cf. Example 3.3.2.

 in this case, $\deg([C_{1}]\cdot[C_{2}])=\deg\mathcal{O}(D)=(C_{1}.C_{2})$, see Section 1.2.1. In Section 3, we shortly return to the intersection product of codimension one cycles and describe its image in $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$.

### 1.2.

The really mysterious part of the Chow ring of a K3 surface is $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$. (See Section 17.2 for a discussion of the group $\mathrm{CH}^{1}(X)\simeq\mathrm{Pic}(X)$.) If $X$ contains a $k$-rational point, then $\deg\colon\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}$ is surjective. Otherwise its image is a finite index subgroup. In any case, the essential part of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ is the kernel $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$.

The following observation, although stated here only for K3 surfaces, holds in full generality, see e.g. *[190, Ex. 1.6.6]*.

###### Proposition 1.2.

If $k$ is algebraically closed, then the group $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ is divisible.

###### Proof.

Clearly, $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ is generated by cycles of the form $[x]-[y]$ with $x,y\in X$. Choose a smooth irreducible curve $x,y\in C\subset X$. Then $\mathcal{O}(x-y)\in\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(C)$. The abelian variety $\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(C)$ is divisible, for multiplication by $n$ defines a finite and hence surjective morphism $\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(C)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(C)$. The push-forward of a divisor corresponding to the $n$-th root of $\mathcal{O}(x-y)$ yields $(1/n)([x]-[y])\in\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$. ∎

The next theorem, originally due to Roitman *[509]*, is much harder. It is again only a special case of a completely general statement that involves the Albanese variety (which is trivial for K3 surfaces).

###### Theorem 1.3.

If $k$ is separably closed, then $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ is torsion free.

###### Proof.

See Roitman’s original article *[509]* and Bloch’s version *[65, 66]* showing that there is no torsion prime to the characteristic. The general statement was established by Milne *[404]*. A brief account was given by Colliot-Thélène in *[120]*, but see also Voisin’s *[617, Sec. 22.1.2]* in the complex setting. ∎

Summarizing, for a K3 surface over an algebraically closed field the Chow groups

$\mathrm{CH}^{0}(X)\simeq\mathbb{Z},\ \mathrm{CH}^{1}(X)\simeq\mathrm{Pic}(X)=\mathrm{NS}(X)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{\rho(X)},\ \mathrm{and}\ \mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$

are torsion free. Moreover, the degree map yields an exact sequence

$0\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0$

with $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ a divisible group.

###### Remark 1.4.

The torsion of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(Y)$ for arbitrary surfaces has been studied intensively. For a survey see *[120]*. We only briefly mention the following results applicable to K3 surfaces. So, we shall assume that $X$ is a K3 surface over an arbitrary field $k$, although the following results hold under more general assumptions.

i) If $\ell$ is prime to the characteristic of $k$, then $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)[\ell^{\infty}]$ (the part of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ annihilated by some power of $\ell$) is a subquotient of $H^{3}_{\acute{e}t}(X,\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}/\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}(2))$, see *[120, Thm. 3.3.2]*.

ii) If $k$ is a finite field, then the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ is finite, cf. *[120, Thm. 5.2]* and *[124]*. See also Proposition 2.16, asserting that in fact $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ is torsion free in this situation.

iii) I am not aware of any finiteness results or instructive examples for the torsion of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)$ for a K3 surface $X$ over a number field or over $\mathbb{F}_{q}(t)$. See the comments at the end of this chapter.

### 1.3.

The *Grothendieck group* $K(Y)$ of a variety (or a noetherian scheme) $Y$ is the free abelian group generated by coherent sheaves $F$ on $Y$ divided by the subgroup generated by elements of the form $[F_{2}]-[F_{1}]-[F_{3}]$ whenever there exists a short exact sequence $0\mathop{\longrightarrow}F_{1}\mathop{\longrightarrow}F_{2}\mathop{\longrightarrow}F_{3}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0$. Elements of $K(Y)$ are represented by finite linear combinations $\sum n_{i}[F_{i}]$ with $n_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $F_{i}\in\mathrm{Coh}(Y)$.

By the very construction, $K(Y)$ is in fact a group that is naturally associated with the abelian category $\mathrm{Coh}(Y)$. Indeed, for an arbitrary abelian category $\mathcal{A}$ one defines its Grothendieck group $K(\mathcal{A})$ as the quotient of the free abelian group generated by objects of $\mathcal{A}$ by the subgroup generated by elements of the form $[A_{2}]-[A_{1}]-[A_{3}]$ for all short exact sequences $0\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{1}\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{2}\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{3}\mathop{\longrightarrow}0$. in particular $[A]=[A^{\prime}]$ in $K(\mathcal{A})$ if $A\simeq A^{\prime}$ and $[A\oplus B]=[A]+[B]$. Thus, clearly

$K(Y)=K(\mathrm{Coh}(Y)).$

There is yet another categorical interpretation of $K(Y)$ which relies on the bounded derived category $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(Y)\coloneqq\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{Coh}(Y))$ viewed as a triangulated category. For an arbitrary (small) triangulated category $\mathcal{D}$ one defines $K(\mathcal{D})$ as the quotient of the free abelian group generated by the objects of $\mathcal{D}$ modulo the subgroup generated by elements of the form $[A_{2}]-[A_{1}]-[A_{3}]$ for all exact triangles $A_{1}\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{2}\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{3}\mathop{\longrightarrow}A_{1}[1]$. For the notion of a triangulated category and, in particular, of exact triangles see *[206, 610]* and Section 16.1.1. Since the identity $A=A$ gives rise to an exact triangle $A\mathop{\longrightarrow}0\mathop{\longrightarrow}A[1]\mathop{\longrightarrow}A[1]$, one has $[A[1]]=-[A]$ for all objects $A$. As any object in the bounded derived category $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{A})$ of an abelian category $\mathcal{A}$ admits a finite filtration with ‘quotients’ isomorphic to shifts of objects in $\mathcal{A}$, there is a natural isomorphism $K(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{A}))\simeq K(\mathcal{A})$. Applied to our case, one finds

$K(Y)=K(\mathrm{Coh}(Y))\simeq K(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(Y)).$

For a smooth and quasi-projective variety $Y$, the Grothendieck group can equivalently be defined as the free abelian group generated by locally free sheaves modulo short exact sequences as before. Indeed, any coherent sheaf on $Y$ admits a finite locally free resolution $0\mathop{\longrightarrow}F_{n}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\ldots\mathop{\longrightarrow}F_{0}\mathop{\longrightarrow}F\mathop{\longrightarrow}0$ and thus $[F]=\sum(-1)^{i}[F_{i}]$. The advantage of working with locally free sheaves only is that the tensor product induces on $K(Y)$ the structure of a commutative ring by

$[F]\cdot[F^{\prime}]\coloneqq[F\otimes F^{\prime}].$

The Grothendieck group and the Chow group can be compared via the *Chern character*. The Chern character defines a ring homomorphism

$\mathrm{ch}\colon K(Y)\mathop{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{CH}^{*}(Y)_{\mathbb{Q}}.$

(Recall that for abelian groups $G$ we use the shorthand $G_{\mathbb{Q}}\coloneqq G\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}$.) The Chern classes $\mathrm{c}_{i}(F)$ of a coherent sheaf $F$ itself are elements in $\mathrm{CH}^{i}(Y)$, but the Chern character $\mathrm{ch}(F)$

has non-trivial denominators in general. However, it induces a ring isomorphism

$\operatorname{ch}\colon K(Y)_{\mathbb{Q}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{CH}^{*}(Y)_{\mathbb{Q}}.$

Observe that $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{O}_{Z})=[Z]\bmod\operatorname{CH}^{*>n}(Y)$ for any subvariety $Z\subset Y$ of codimension $n$.

### 1.4.

Let us come back to the case of a K3 surface $X$. Then the Chern character of a sheaf $F$ on $X$ is given as

$\operatorname{ch}(F)=\operatorname{rk}(F)+\operatorname{c}_{1}(F)+\frac{(\operatorname{c}_{1}^{2}-2\operatorname{c}_{2})(F)}{2}.$

Here, $\operatorname{rk}(F)$ is the dimension of the fibre of $F$ at the generic point $\eta\in X$, i.e. $\operatorname{rk}(F)=\dim_{K(X)}(F_{\eta})$, and $\operatorname{c}_{1}(F)=\operatorname{c}_{1}(\det(F))$. If $F$ is globally generated and locally of rank two, then $\operatorname{c}_{2}(F)$ can be represented by $[Z(s)]$, where $Z(s)$ is the zero locus of a regular section $s\in H^{0}(X,F)$. Proposition 1.2 can be used to show that Chern characters of sheaves on K3 surfaces are in fact integral, at least for $k=\bar{k}$.

###### Corollary 1.5.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over an algebraically closed field $k$. Then the Chern character naturally defines an isomorphism of rings

$\operatorname{ch}\colon K(X)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{CH}^{*}(X).$

###### Proof.

By the Riemann–Roch formula $\deg(\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)^{2})=(L)^{2}$ is even. Thus, for algebraically closed $k$ it is divisible by two in the image of the surjection $\deg\colon\operatorname{CH}^{2}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathbb{Z}$. On the other hand, by Proposition 1.2 the kernel of $\deg$, i.e. $\operatorname{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$, is divisible for $k=\bar{k}$ and hence $(1/2)\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)^{2}$ exists uniquely, due to the absence of torsion in $\operatorname{CH}^{2}(X)$, see Theorem 1.3.

Next we prove that $\operatorname{ch}\colon K(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\operatorname{CH}^{*}(X)$ is surjective. Indeed, the generator $1=[X]$ of $\operatorname{CH}^{0}(X)$ equals $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{O}_{X})$ and $[x]=\operatorname{ch}(k(x))$ for all closed points $x\in X$. Thus $\operatorname{CH}^{0}(X)\oplus\operatorname{CH}^{2}(X)$ is contained in the image. As $(1/2)\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)^{2}\in\operatorname{CH}^{2}(X)$ for all $L\in\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(L)=1+\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)+(1/2)\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)^{2}$, all first Chern classes $\operatorname{c}_{1}(L)$ are in the image of the Chern character, i.e. $\operatorname{CH}^{1}(X)\subset\operatorname{Im}(\operatorname{ch})$.

To prove injectivity, one shows that for any smooth surface $Y$ there are natural isomorphisms

$\operatorname{rk}\colon F^{0}K(Y)/F^{1}K(Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{Z},$
$\operatorname{c}_{1}\colon F^{1}K(Y)/F^{2}K(Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{Pic}(Y),\text{ and }\operatorname{c}_{2}\colon F^{2}K(Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{CH}^{2}(Y).$

Here, $F^{i}K(Y)$ is the subgroup generated by sheaves with support of codimension $\geq i$. In particular, $\operatorname{ch}\colon K(Y)\!\longrightarrow\!\operatorname{CH}^{*}(Y)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is always injective. See *[190, Ex. 15.3.6]*. ∎

It would be interesting to find a direct proof for the torsion freeness of $K(X)$.

## 2. Chow groups: Mumford and Bloch–Beĭlinson

After these general results, we now pass to things that are more specific to K3 surfaces. In fact, although we shall state the results for K3 surfaces only, often the condition $p_{g}(X)\coloneqq h^{0}(X,\omega_{X})>0$ suffices.

###

.

### 2.1.

We start with a celebrated result of Mumford for K3 surfaces over $\mathbb{C}$ (or over any uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic zero). In *[437]* he disproves an old claim of Severi that the group of $0$-cycles modulo rational equivalence is always finite-dimensional by showing that the dimension of the image of the natural map

$\sigma_{n}\colon X^{n}\times X^{n}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0},\;((x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}))\longmapsto\sum\left([x_{i}]-[y_{i}]\right)$

cannot be bounded. To make this precise, we need a few preparations. See *[617]* for details and more general results.

Clearly, the map $\sigma_{n}\colon X^{n}\times X^{n}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ factorizes over the symmetric product

$\sigma_{n}\colon S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$

and we shall rather work with the latter.

###### Proposition 2.1.

The fibres of the map $\sigma_{n}\colon S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ are countable unions of closed subvarieties. Moreover, there exists a countable union $Y\subset S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X)$ of proper subvarieties such that for all points $(Z_{1},Z_{2})$ in the complement of $Y$ the maximal dimension of $\sigma_{n}^{-1}\sigma_{n}(Z_{1},Z_{2})$ is constant.

###### Proof.

The very rough idea goes as follows. Cycles $Z_{1},Z_{2}\in S^{n}(X)$ that define the same class $\alpha\in\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ are obtained by adding cycles of the form $\mathrm{div}_{0}(f)+D$ and $\mathrm{div}_{\infty}(f)+D$ to $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$, respectively. Here, $f$ is a rational function on some curve $C$ in $X$, $\mathrm{div}_{0}(f)$ and $\mathrm{div}_{\infty}(f)$ are its zero and pole divisor, and $D$ is just some divisor on $C$.

These data are parametrized by certain Hilbert schemes and thus form a countable set of varieties. For more details see *[617, Lem. 22.7]*. ∎

Let now $f_{n}$ be the dimension of the generic fibre $\sigma_{n}^{-1}\sigma_{n}(Z_{1},Z_{2})$ in the sense of the proposition. Although the image of $\sigma_{n}$ does not have the structure of a variety, one can talk about its dimension.

###### Definition 2.2.

The image dimension of $\sigma$ is defined as

$\dim(\mathrm{Im}(\sigma_{n}))\coloneqq\dim(S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X))-f_{n}=4n-f_{n}.$

The following result then says that the ‘dimension’ of $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ is infinite.

###### Theorem 2.3 (Mumford).

For a complex K3 surface $X$ one has

$\lim\dim(\mathrm{Im}(\sigma_{n}))=\infty.$

###### Proof.

The key idea is the following. The fibres of $\sigma_{n}$ are countable unions of subvarieties. The generator of $H^{0}(X,\Omega_{X}^{2})$ induces a non-degenerate regular two-form on $X^{n}\times X^{n}$ which is symmetric and hence descends to a generically non-degenerate two-form on $S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X)$. (Restrict to the smooth part to avoid the singularities.) Morally (but not literally!), the components of the fibres of $\sigma_{n}$ tend to be rationally connected, for they parametrize rationally equivalent cycles. Since a rationally connected variety does not admit any non-trivial two-form (see *[310, IV Cor. 3.8]*), the components of the fibres should be of dimension at most $(1/2)\dim(S^{n}(X)\times S^{n}(X))$. ∎

2. CHOW GROUPS: MUMFORD AND BLOCH-BEILINSON

Remark 2.4. It turns out that for general surfaces  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_0$  is finite dimensional if and only if  $\sigma_{n}$  is surjective for large  $n$ , see [617, Prop. 22.10]. Furthermore, this condition for a K3 surface is equivalent to  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_0 = 0$  or, still equivalent, to  $\operatorname {Jac}(C)\longrightarrow \operatorname {CH}^2 (X)_0$  for some ample curve  $C\subset X$ . The latter is the notion of finite-dimensionality used by Bloch in [66]. So K3 surfaces over  $\mathbb{C}$  have infinite dimensional  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)$ .

2.2. In contrast to Mumford's result for K3 surfaces over  $\mathbb{C}$  (or, more generally, uncountable algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero) the situation is expected to be completely different for K3 surfaces over global fields, e.g. over number fields.

Conjecture 2.5 (Bloch-Beilinson). If  $X$  is a  $K3$  surface over a number field  $k$  (i.e. a finite field extension of  $\mathbb{Q}$ ), then the degree map defines an isomorphism

$$
\mathrm {C H} ^ {2} (X) _ {\mathbb {Q}} \simeq \mathbb {Q}.
$$

If  $X$  is a  $K3$  surface over  $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)\simeq \mathbb{Z}$ .

This is only a special case of much deeper conjectures generalizing the conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer for elliptic curves, see [55, 67, 501]. However, there is essentially no evidence for this conjecture. There is not a single K3 surface  $X$  known that is defined over a number field and has  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\simeq \mathbb{Q}$ . In fact, it seems we do not even have examples where any kind of finiteness result for  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_0$  has been established. As shall be briefly mentioned below,  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_0$  often contains torsion classes which after base change to  $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$  become trivial.

Remark 2.6. It is expected that the conjecture fails when one replaces  $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$  by the minimal algebraically closed field of definition. But to the best of my knowledge, there has never been given an explicit example for this, i.e. there does not seem to be known an example of a K3 surface  $X$  defined over an algebraically closed field  $k$  with  $\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}(k) &gt; 0$  and not over any field of smaller transcendence degree with  $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)\neq \mathbb{Z}$ .

Remark 2.7. There is a different set of finiteness conjectures due to Bass. $^3$ For a smooth projective variety $X$ over a field $k$ which is finitely generated over its prime field, the Grothendieck group $K(X)$ is conjectured to be finitely generated, see [34, Chap. XIII]. this in particular predicts that for a K3 surface over a number field $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)$ should be finitely generated, but (up to torsion) the conjecture of Bloch-Beilinson is more precise. A priori Bass's conjectures do not explain why passing from a number field to $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ the rank of $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)$ does not increase. On the other hand, Bass's conjectures also predict that $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)$ is finitely generated for fields which are finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ or $\mathbb{F}_p(t_1,t_2)$ (or other purely transcendental extensions of the prime field of finite transcendence degree). Compare this to the results in Sections 2.3 and 2.4.

$^2$In [277, App. B] one finds an example due to Schoen of a K3 surface  $X$  over some finite extension of  $\mathbb{Q}(t)$  that cannot be defined over  $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$  and for which  $\mathrm{CH}^2(X)_0$  is of infinite rank. However, this example becomes isotrivial after passing to the algebraic closure of  $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ . Thanks to Stefan Schreieder for pointing this out.

12. CHOW RING AND GROTHENDIECK GROUP

Example 2.8.

 while we do not have a single example confirming the Bloch–Beilinson conjecture, we have plenty of examples confirming the conjecture of Bass. For example, it is not difficult to show that $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)\simeq \mathbb{Z}$ for the generic fibre $X\coloneqq \mathcal{X}_{\eta}$ of the universal quartic $\mathcal{X}\subset |\mathcal{O}(4)|\times \mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{Q}}^3$. So, here the base field is the finitely generated field $k(\eta) = \mathbb{Q}(t_1,\ldots,t_{34})$. Note also, that considering the same situation over $\mathbb{C}$ yields an example of a K3 surface with $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)\simeq \mathbb{Z}$ over the field $\mathbb{C}(t_1,\dots,t_{34})$, which certainly is not finitely generated.

2.3. The Chow group can change under base field extension. Suppose a K3 surface $X$ is defined over a field $k$ and $k \subset K$ is a field extension. The pull-back defines a natural homomorphism

$$
\mathrm{CH}^* (X) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^* (X_K),\ Z \longmapsto Z_K.
$$

Clearly, $\mathrm{CH}^0 (X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{CH}^0 (X_K)$ and $\mathrm{CH}^1 (X)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^1 (X_K)$, see Section 17.2.1. In degree two the map is in general neither injective nor surjective. However, its kernel is purely torsion, due to the following easy

Lemma 2.9. For any field extension $k \subset K$ the pull-back map

$$
\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}
$$

is injective.

Proof. Consider first a finite extension $k \subset K$. Then the natural projection $\pi \colon X_K \longrightarrow X$ is a finite morphism of degree $[K : k]$ and thus satisfies

$$
\pi_* \pi^* \alpha = [K : k] \cdot \alpha
$$

for all $\alpha \in \mathrm{CH}^*(X)$. This is a special case of the projection formula, see e.g. [234, p. 426]. Hence, if $\pi^*\alpha \in \mathrm{CH}^2(X_K)$ is zero, then $\alpha \in \mathrm{CH}^2(X)$ was at least torsion. This proves the result for any finite (and then also for any algebraic) field extension. Below we reduce the general result to this case.

Let now $k \subset K$ be an arbitrary field extension $k \subset K$. If $Z \in \mathrm{CH}^2(X)$ is in the kernel of the pull-back $\mathrm{CH}^2(X) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^2(X_K)$, then $Z$ becomes trivial after a finitely generated field extension $k \subset L \subset K$. Indeed, the rational equivalence making $Z_K$ trivial over $K$ involves only finitely many curves $C_i$ and rational functions on them. The finitely many coefficients needed to define these curves with the rational functions generate a field $L$. In fact, we may assume that $L$ is the quotient field of a finitely generated $k$-algebra $A$ and the curves $C_i$ are defined over $A$. Now think of $X_L$ as the generic fibre of the 'spread' $X \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(A) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(A)$. In particular, for any closed point $a \in \operatorname{Spec}(A)$ the restriction of $Z_{\operatorname{Spec}(A)}$ to the fibre $X \times \operatorname{Spec}(k(a))$ is rationally equivalent to zero by means of the restriction of the curves $C_i$. As $k(a)$ is a finite field extension of $k$ and the restriction of $Z_{\operatorname{Spec}(A)}$ to the fibre over $a$ is nothing but $Z_{k(a)}$, this shows by step one that $Z$ was torsion.

4We emphasize again, that no explicit examples of K3 surfaces over a number field seems to be known for which $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)$ is finitely generated.

2. CHOW GROUPS: MUMFORD AND BLOCH-BEILINSON

 for finite Galois extensions $K / k$ with Galois group $G$, the cokernel of the base-change map $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)\longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)^G$ is torsion (see [120, §2] and compare this to the discussion in Section 17.2.2), i.e.

$$
\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}^G.
$$

The following result due to Bloch, see [66].

**Proposition 2.10.** Let $X$ be a K3 surface over an arbitrary field $k$ such that $\rho(X \times_k \bar{k}) &lt; 22$. If $K = k(X)$ denotes the function field of $X$, then

$$
\mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}
$$

is not surjective.

**Proof.** The construction of an extra cycle is very explicit. Consider the diagonal $\Delta \subset X \times X$ and its restriction $\Delta_K$ to the generic fibre $X_K = X \times \operatorname{Spec}(K) \subset X \times X$ of the second projection. One now proves that $[\Delta_K] \in \mathrm{CH}^2(X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not contained in $\mathrm{CH}^2(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$. For this, one can certainly pass to the algebraic closure of $k$ and, therefore, we may simply assume $k = \bar{k}$.

Suppose it was, i.e. $[\Delta_K] = \sum n_i[x_i]$ in $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ for certain $n_i \in \mathbb{Q}$ and closed points $x_i \in X$ with their associated classes $[x_i] \in \mathrm{CH}^2 (X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \subset \mathrm{CH}^2 (X_K)_{\mathbb{Q}}$. In other words, there exist curves $C_i \subset X_K$ and rational functions $f_i \in K(C_i)$ such that $\Delta_K = \sum n_i x_i + \sum \mathrm{div}_{C_i}(f_i)$ as cycles on $X_K \subset X \times X$. Taking the closure in $X \times X$ yields

$$
\Delta = \sum n_i (\{x_i\} \times X) + \sum D_i + V \tag{2.1}
$$

as cycles on $X \times X$. Here, $V \subset X \times X$ does not meet the generic fibre (and therefore does not dominate the second factor) and $D_i \coloneqq \mathrm{div}_{\bar{C}_i}(f_i)$ with $\bar{C}_i$ the closure of $C_i$.

Both sides of the equation can be viewed as cohomological correspondences. In characteristic zero one could pass to the associated complex surfaces and use singular cohomology. Otherwise use $\ell$-adic étale cohomology, $\ell \neq \mathrm{char}(k)$.

Clearly, $[\Delta]_*$ is the identity on $H_{\ell \ell}^2(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell(1))$. On the other hand, $[\{x_i\} \times X]_*$ acts trivially on $H_{\ell \ell}^2(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell(1))$ for degree reasons and the $D_i$ are rationally and hence homologically trivial. Thus, $\mathrm{id} = [\Delta]_* = [V]_*$.

Under the assumption $\rho(X) &lt; 22$, the first Chern class induces a proper inclusion $\mathrm{NS}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}_\ell} \subset H_{\ell \ell}^2(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell(1))$, cf. Section 17.2.2. Since the image of $V$ under the second projection is supported in dimension $\leq 1$, the image of $[V]_*$ is contained in $\mathrm{NS}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}$. Contradiction.

**Remark 2.11.** Clearly, in characteristic zero the assumption on the Picard group is superfluous. One always has $\rho(X \times_k \bar{k}) \leq 20$, which can be proved by Hodge theory over $\mathbb{C}$, see Sections 1.3.3 or 17.1.1.

However, for K3 surfaces in positive characteristic the case $\rho(X \times_k \bar{k}) = 22$ may occur and the above argument breaks down. In fact, it was conjectured and has now been proved

5At this point one uses that the cycle map factors through the Chow ring and, in this case more precisely, that $\mathrm{CH}^2 (X\times X)\longrightarrow H_{\ell \ell}^2 (X\times X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell (2))$ is well-defined.

by Liedtke in *[371]* that for a K3 surface $X$ the condition $\rho(X\times_{k}\bar{k})=22$ is equivalent to $X$ being unirational, see Proposition 17.2.7 and Section 18.3.5. Any unirational surface satisfies $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\simeq\mathbb{Q}$ and, since a unirational variety remains unirational after base change, the Chow group does indeed not grow after passage to $X_{k(X)}$ or any other field extension.

As an immediate consequence, we obtain the following weak form of Mumford’s result, cf. Theorem 2.3.

###### Corollary 2.12.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over $\mathbb{C}$. Then $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}=\infty$.

###### Proof.

Indeed, $X$ is defined over the algebraic closure $k_{0}$ of a finitely generated extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e. $X=X_{0}\times_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}$, and by choosing inductively $k_{i}$ to be the algebraic closure of $K(X_{0}\times_{k_{0}}k_{i-1})$ and embeddings $k_{0}\subset k_{1}\subset\ldots\subset\mathbb{C}$ one obtains a strictly ascending chain of vector spaces

$\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X_{0})_{\mathbb{Q}}\subsetneq\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X_{0}\times_{k_{0}}k_{1})_{\mathbb{Q}}\subsetneq\ldots\subsetneq\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X_{0}\times_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C})_{\mathbb{Q}}.$

###### Remark 2.13.

i) The same arguments show that for every K3 surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of infinite transcendence degree over its prime field, one has $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}=\infty$ provided that $\rho(X)<22$.

ii) In fact, Bloch uses similar methods to prove the full result of Mumford, i.e. that there is no curve $C\subset X$ (possibly disconnected) such that $\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(C)\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{0}$ is surjective, cf. Remark 2.4. For details see *[66, App. Lect. 1]*.

In characteristic zero, an analogous construction can be used to show that the Chow group increases already after base change to an algebraically closed field of transcendence degree one. The following is based on the paper by Green, Griffiths, and Paranjape *[215]* and works more generally for surfaces with $p_{g}\neq 0$.

###### Proposition 2.14.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over a field $k$ of characteristic zero. If $K$ is an algebraically closed extension of $k$ with $\mathrm{trdeg}_{k}(K)\geq 1$, then

$\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X_{K})_{\mathbb{Q}}$

is not surjective.

###### Proof.

Similar to the proof of Proposition 2.10, one constructs a certain cycle $Z\subset X\times C$, whose generic fibre over $C$ defines a class that is not contained in the image of the pull-back $\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathrm{CH}^{2}(X_{k(C)})_{\mathbb{Q}}$. Here, $C$ is a smooth curve with function field $k(C)$. For the following we can assume that $k$ is algebraically closed of finite transcendence degree with an embedding $k\subset\mathbb{C}$, which allows us to use Hodge theory for the complex manifolds $X_{\mathbb{C}}$ and $C_{\mathbb{C}}$.

The cycle $Z$ is constructed as follows. Firstly, consider the diagonal $\Delta\subset X\times X$ and its action $[\Delta]_{*}$ on $H^{*}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})$. In degree two it respects the decomposition $H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})=\mathrm{Pic}(X_{\mathbb{C}})_{\mathbb{Q}}\oplus T(X_{\mathbb{C}})_{\mathbb{Q}}$. Here, $T(X_{\mathbb{C}})$ is the transcendental lattice, cf. Section 3.2.2. On $\mathrm{Pic}(X_{\mathbb{C}})_{\mathbb{Q}}$ one can describe $[\Delta]_{*}$ as the action of a cycle of the form $\sum m_{i}(C_{i}\times D_{i})$ with

curves $C_{i},D_{i}\subset X$ and $m_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}$. Since $\mathrm{Pic}(X)\simeq\mathrm{Pic}(X_{\mathbb{C}})$ (cf. Lemma 17.2.2), we may assume that indeed these curves exist over $k$. Now, fix a closed point $x\in X$ and let

$Y\coloneqq\Delta-\sum m_{i}(C_{i}\times D_{i})-\{x\}\times X.$

Viewed as a correspondence from the second to the first factor, it acts trivially on $H^{4}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})$ and $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$ and as the identity on the transcendental part $T(X_{\mathbb{C}})$. Now pick a smooth curve $C\subset X$ and let $Z$ be the pull-back of $Y$ under the natural inclusion $X\times C\subset X\times X$.

One checks that $Z$ is homologically trivial, i.e. $0=[Z]_{*}\colon H^{*}(C_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})\!\longrightarrow\!H^{*}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})$. For example, for the generator $[C]\in H^{0}(C_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Z})$ one computes, using the projection formula, that $[Z]_{*}[C]=[Y]_{*}[C]$, where on the right hand side $[C]\in H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Z})$ is contained in the Picard group and hence $[Y]_{*}[C]=0$. A similar argument works for the generator of $H^{2}(C_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Z})$.
